title: A man in the land of Uz (Job 1:1–12)
hook: a blameless man, and the adversary's question: does he serve for nothing?

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ruth the Moabitess became the great-grandmother of King David. Your line was a cradle and a king. Whose name did you say out loud? Today, a new book in the Writings: Job. Day eight hundred thirty-eight.

"There was a man in the land of Uz, whose name was Job." That's how it opens, like a story told at bedtime. No king's name, no year, no map. The book never says where Uz is. The man is good, the text says, perfect and upright, one who feared God and turned away from evil. He has sons and daughters, flocks and herds, a full house. His children throw feasts, taking turns at each other's homes, and after every round Job gets up early and offers sacrifices for them, just in case one of them sinned and cursed God in their heart. A careful father. A man with nothing to hide. And then the scene changes, and we're not in Uz anymore.
screen: `A MAN IN THE LAND OF UZ.` → `PERFECT AND UPRIGHT.` → `UP EARLY FOR HIS CHILDREN.`

segments.voice: We're in heaven, at a gathering before God, and one of those who comes is called, in Hebrew, ha-satan. The word has "the" in front of it: the adversary, the accuser. Here he isn't a ruler of his own kingdom. He shows up with the others and answers to God. God speaks first: "Hast thou considered my servant Job, that there is none like him in the earth?" And the adversary asks the question the whole book will live inside: "Doth Job fear God for nought?" For nothing. Look at the fence you've put around him, he says. His house, his work, his flocks. Take it away, and he'll curse you to your face. And God allows it: everything Job has is in your hand, but don't touch the man himself. Then the adversary goes out, and Job knows none of this. That's the strange gift of this book. We, the readers, know why it's happening. Job never does. Some readers hear the question turned on themselves. Is goodness a deal? Am I kind because it works, honest because it pays, faithful because life has gone well? Or is there something underneath that would still be there if the rewards stopped? The rabbis didn't agree on who Job was. In the Talmud, one teacher says Job never lived at all, that the book is a parable, and others argue for different ages and places. Either way, the question lands on the reader. Uz could be anywhere. The man could be anyone.
screen: `HA-SATAN: THE ADVERSARY.` · `DOTH JOB FEAR GOD FOR NOUGHT?` · `WE KNOW WHY. JOB NEVER DOES.` · `A REAL MAN, OR A PARABLE?`

segments.voice: Today, sit with one unfair question. Settle, and breathe. Let the adversary's question come close, turned gently toward your own life. Pick one good thing you do: calling your mother, showing up to work honest, giving, praying, being patient with a kid. Then ask it quietly: would I still do this if nothing came back? Don't answer. Don't defend yourself. Don't decide you're a fraud or a saint. Just let the question sit in the room with you, the way it sits at the start of this book, unanswered. Breathe in, and hold it. Breathe out, and let it stay. If you pray, you can bring the question to God as it is. The bell holds the time.
ha-satan, the Hebrew name, with "the" in front of it, for the adversary who comes before God and asks whether Job fears God for nothing. Today's word.
Your line: is it for nothing. Today, do one good thing nobody will see or thank you for, and notice how it feels to do it for nothing. Day eight hundred thirty-eight.

howItsDone: Job is one of the books of the Writings, the third part of the Tanakh. Jews study it as a book of wisdom and argument about suffering, and traditional study includes the rabbis' debate over whether Job was a real man or a parable.

original.note: Hebrew: for nothing, freely; the word in the adversary's question in Job 1:9.

trapdoor: what you thought: the devil makes a bet with God.
what it means: ha-satan, the adversary, answers to God and asks whether anyone is good for nothing.
what a scholar hears: in the Talmud, one rabbi says Job never lived and the book is a parable, while others place him in different ages.

notes: Job 1:2–3 gives seven sons, three daughters and exact herd counts; the script leaves the numbers out.
Ha-satan with the definite article read as 'the adversary/accuser', a member of the heavenly court rather than the later devil figure: please confirm the framing is right for this path.
Bava Batra 15a: the view that Job 'never was and never existed, but was a parable' is paraphrased; other rabbis there date Job to various periods. Please confirm.
'Is goodness a deal?' is offered as the reader's question, not a claim about the text.

Editor: replaced the narrator's 'It's about all of us' with an attributed 'Some readers hear the question turned on themselves', so the script doesn't tell the listener what the question means for them.
